TLR2 is able to trigger type I interferon induction from endolysosomal compartment.
TLR2, which is a cell surface receptor and a major sensor of bacterial infections, is able to induce interferon-beta responses from endolysosomal compartment.

In summary, our research is concerned with
how the immune system recognizes and responds to microbes.
the molecular mechanisms of innate immunity, in particular how the immune system recognizes microbial pathogens and how this leads to the induction of immune responses.
understanding the cellular pathways involved in host defense against microbial infection and how these pathways are modulated to prevent or control inflammation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the TLR2 sub-family of TLRs, which recognizes a broad range of microbial components, is capable of triggering pro-inflammatory responses at the plasma membrane, and type I interferons from endolysosomal sites.
TLR2, as other TLRs, can activate the type I interferon response.
TLR2 signaling induces type I interferons from the endolysosomal compartment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TLR2 signaling can be regulated at the subcellular level.
we have discovered that TLR2 can trigger two distinct responses, one at the cell surface and the other in endolysosomes.
TLR2 is a sensor for both extracellular and endosomal microbes and that TLR2 dependent type I IFN production occurs from endolysosomes and is independent of receptor internalization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TLR2 is able to activate both pro-inflammatory cytokine and type I interferons pathways.
TLR2 is able to induce type I interferon production and this is a novel pathway for the induction of type I IFNs.
